note: Shapes that SimpleDiagrams resolves by reference. A symbol_reference uses library_id, item_id and the library's asset_version exactly as listed.

shapes.description: A simple person icon for a man.
A male customer shown with a crown.
A simple person icon for a woman.
A female customer shown with a crown.
A crown for royalty, leadership or authority.
A small group of people working together.
A group of people involved in a task or decision.
Two curved arrows showing an exchange or repeated interaction.
An office building shown in perspective.
A taller office building shown in perspective.
A banknote marked with a dollar sign.
A check mark in a box for a completed, correct or approved item.
A cross in a box for a wrong, rejected or incomplete item.
An analogue clock for time or scheduling.
A desktop computer for office work and information technology.
A cylinder representing a database or stored information.
A form with fields for collecting information.
A pain point or problem, shown by a lightning bolt and pointer.
A checklist of tasks with some items ticked off.
A sheet of paper representing a document or report.
Office binders for storing paperwork.
A coin marked with the euro sign.
A coin marked with the dollar sign, for dollar-denominated currencies.
A coin marked with the pound sterling sign.
A coin marked with the yen sign: Japanese money.
A coin marked with the yuan character: Chinese money, the renminbi.
A coin marked Fr, for francs: Swiss money.
A blank coin for money, a token or an unspecified currency.
The person who started the company and sets its direction.
A software engineer: someone who writes and ships the code.
A product or brand designer, shaping how the product looks and works.
A product manager: decides what gets built next and why.
Someone who puts money into the company in return for a share of it.
A recruiter or people-team member finding and hiring candidates.
A support agent answering customers and resolving their requests.
A short daily team meeting at the task board: what was done, what is next, what is blocked.
Who reports to whom: the company's reporting lines, level by level.
A regular private conversation between two people, usually a manager and one of their team.
A meeting of the whole company, where leaders share results and news with everyone at once.
A meeting held over video, with each person shown in their own tile on screen.
Finding and adding a new person to the team to fill an open role.
A new starter's first days: getting their pass, accounts and a checklist of things to learn.
A regular written assessment of how well someone is doing their job, with ratings and goals.
A session where a team puts up as many ideas as it can before choosing the best ones.
A team whose members work together from different cities or countries.
The first outside money a young company raises, to get from an idea to a product.
One stage of raising money from investors; each later round is usually larger than the last.
A short document setting out the main terms of an investment before the contracts are written.
The list of who owns how much of the company: founders, investors and staff.
How fast a company is spending its cash each month, before it earns enough to cover its costs.
Income that comes in again every month or year from subscriptions, not from one-off sales.
A customer paying for something by tapping a card on a phone or reader.
A bill sent to a customer, listing what was supplied and the total amount owed.
Paying everyone in the company their salary or wages on a regular schedule.
The tiers a product is sold in, each with its own features and price, one of them recommended.
A board of work items moving through columns from to-do to done.
An AI assistant answering a question in a chat.
A timeline of what the team plans to build and when, showing work in progress and milestones.
A short, fixed period, often two weeks, in which a team finishes a set batch of work, then repeats.
The ordered list of work waiting to be done, with the most important items at the top.
Putting a new product or feature in front of customers for the first time.
A packaged version of the software shipped to production, where customers use it.
A switch that turns a feature on or off for chosen users without shipping new code.
An experiment that shows two versions to different users and measures which one performs better.
What customers say about the product: their ratings, reviews and comments.
The steps a customer goes through, from first hearing of the product to reaching their goal.
A connection that lets two systems or apps exchange data automatically.
One screen of charts and numbers that shows how the business is doing at a glance.
Keeping the product, its data and its customers' accounts safe from misuse.
Growth that starts flat and then takes off: the hockey-stick curve.
The steps people pass through on the way to becoming customers, with fewer left at each step.
A growth loop where each part feeds the next, so every turn makes the following one easier.
The one number a company steers by, because it best shows that customers are getting value.
Objectives and key results: one goal and the few measurable results that show progress towards it.
Customers who stop using or paying for the product in a given period.
How many customers keep coming back over time, tracked group by group in a cohort chart.
A product that becomes more useful to everyone each time another person joins.
A deliberate change of direction after the first plan did not work out.
A grid that sorts options by two measures at once, so the best ones stand out in one corner.
The point where a product clearly meets a need that enough customers have.
Deals moving stage by stage from first contact to a closed sale, with fewer left at each stage.
A platform that brings buyers and sellers together and handles the exchange between them.
A profile of a typical customer: who they are, what they want and how they behave.
Where the process starts.
The process starts when a message arrives.
The process starts when a set time is reached or a period has passed.
The process starts when a condition becomes true.
The process starts when a signal is broadcast.
The process starts when any one of several things happens.
The process starts when an error is raised. Used as the start of an event sub-process.
The process starts when earlier work has to be undone. Used as the start of an event sub-process.
The process starts when an escalation is raised. Used as the start of an event sub-process.
The process starts when all of several things have happened.
Starts an event sub-process when a message arrives, without stopping the work already under way.
Starts an event sub-process when a set time is reached or a period has passed, without stopping the work already under way.
Starts an event sub-process when a condition becomes true, without stopping the work already under way.
Starts an event sub-process when a signal is broadcast, without stopping the work already under way.
Starts an event sub-process when any one of several things happens, without stopping the work already under way.
Starts an event sub-process when an escalation is raised, without stopping the work already under way.
Starts an event sub-process when all of several things have happened, without stopping the work already under way.
Something that happens partway through the process.
The flow waits here until a message arrives. Placed on the edge of a task, it takes over from the task when that happens.
The flow waits here until a set time is reached or a period has passed. Placed on the edge of a task, it takes over from the task when that happens.
The flow waits here until an error is raised. Placed on the edge of a task, it takes over from the task when that happens.
The flow waits here until a transaction is cancelled. Placed on the edge of a task, it takes over from the task when that happens.
The flow waits here until earlier work has to be undone. Placed on the edge of a task, it takes over from the task when that happens.
The flow waits here until a condition becomes true. Placed on the edge of a task, it takes over from the task when that happens.
The flow waits here until the flow arrives from a matching link elsewhere on the page. Placed on the edge of a task, it takes over from the task when that happens.
The flow waits here until a signal is broadcast. Placed on the edge of a task, it takes over from the task when that happens.
The flow waits here until any one of several things happens. Placed on the edge of a task, it takes over from the task when that happens.
The flow waits here until an escalation is raised. Placed on the edge of a task, it takes over from the task when that happens.
The flow waits here until all of several things have happened. Placed on the edge of a task, it takes over from the task when that happens.
Placed on the edge of a task: when a message arrives, a side branch starts and the task carries on.
Placed on the edge of a task: when a set time is reached or a period has passed, a side branch starts and the task carries on.
Placed on the edge of a task: when a condition becomes true, a side branch starts and the task carries on.
Placed on the edge of a task: when a signal is broadcast, a side branch starts and the task carries on.
Placed on the edge of a task: when any one of several things happens, a side branch starts and the task carries on.
Placed on the edge of a task: when an escalation is raised, a side branch starts and the task carries on.

shapes.display_name: Parallel multiple intermediate event, catching, non-interrupting
shapes.description: Placed on the edge of a task: when all of several things have happened, a side branch starts and the task carries on.
The process sends a message here and carries on.
The process asks for earlier work to be undone here and carries on.
The process jumps to a matching link elsewhere on the page here and carries on.
The process broadcasts a signal here and carries on.
The process sends several things at once here and carries on.
The process raises an escalation here and carries on.
This path of the process ends here.
This path of the process ends and sends a message.
This path of the process ends and raises an error.
This path of the process ends and cancels the transaction.
This path of the process ends and asks for earlier work to be undone.
This path of the process ends and broadcasts a signal.
This path of the process ends and stops every other path of the process at once.
This path of the process ends and sends several things at once.
This path of the process ends and raises an escalation.
A decision: the flow takes exactly one of the paths leaving it.
The flow takes whichever path's event happens first.
Starts a new process when the first of several events happens.
The flow takes every path whose condition is true, one or more.
The flow splits to follow every path at once, or waits for all of them to arrive.
Starts a new process once all of several events have happened.
A split or join with a rule of its own, explained in a note.
Work done by a system or service, with nobody involved.
The process waits here for a message to arrive.
The process sends a message.
Work a person does with the help of software, such as filling in a form.
A script the process engine runs itself.
Work a person does by hand, without any system.
A message arriving here starts a new process.
A decision worked out from a set of business rules.
A step that is a whole process in itself, folded shut. Its detail is drawn elsewhere.
A step that calls a process defined somewhere else, so it can be reused.
A sub-process that is started by an event and not by the flow reaching it.
A sub-process that either finishes as a whole or is undone as a whole.
Placed at the bottom of a task: the task repeats until a condition is met.
Placed at the bottom of a task: the task is done several times at once, once for each item.
Placed at the bottom of a task: the task is done several times, one after another, once for each item.
Placed at the bottom of a task: the task undoes work done earlier.
Placed at the bottom of a sub-process: its steps can be done in any order.
Placed at the bottom of a task to show it is a sub-process folded shut.
A piece of information the process uses or produces, such as an order or a report.
A set of the same kind of information, such as a list of orders.
Information the process needs from outside before it can start, such as an application form. Its arrow is outlined.
A set of the same kind of information the process needs from outside, such as a batch of claims.
Information the process hands back when it finishes, such as an approved order. Its arrow is solid.
A set of the same kind of information the process hands back, such as a list of invoices.
Somewhere information is kept beyond the life of the process, such as a database.
A message passed between two participants. This one starts the conversation.
A message sent in reply to an earlier one.
For a conversation diagram: the messages two or more participants exchange about one thing, such as an order, shown as one exchange. Lines join it to each participant's pool.
A conversation defined somewhere else and reused here. Its border is heavy, like a call activity's.
A note for the reader. Its text sits to the right of the bracket.
A frame that gathers shapes for the reader. It changes nothing about how the process runs.
